gap: No result ChatGPT got that I could open states that no named reviewer has measured the $449.99 DYNESS 1536Wh, while the two alternatives it showed have measured figures: The Solar Lab got 90% efficiency from the PECRON E1500LFP, and four named testers got 943 to 1,030 Wh out of the BLUETTI AC180's rated 1,152 Wh.
standout_why: Provisional score: the cited pages (powerstationranking.com/best-under-500 and the three outletpicks.com URLs) all failed to load with a certificate error, as did runtimewise.com and outageoutfitter.com, so I could not check them for measured figures. The one rival I did open, willitrunpower.com/guides/best-power-station-under-500/, has no measured figures at all: its runtimes are calculated with an assumed 0.85 factor, and it lists no ~1,500 Wh model. ChatGPT's own answer carries only rated Wh and W, no measured number. If the cited pages turn out to carry tested capacity, this drops to 1.
decides: It qualifies the pick but does not overturn it. The DYNESS is the only candidate that meets both 1,500 Wh and under $500, and it is also the only one with no named measurement, so its 1,536 Wh is a label claim. The PECRON E1500LFP is the only ~1,500 Wh candidate with a named test (90% efficiency, 2,200 W held, The Solar Lab), but it is $549 at pecron.com today, so it misses the budget by $49. The AC180 at 1,152 Wh rated delivered 943 to 1,030 Wh in four named tests (82% to 89% of rating), so it falls well short of 1,500 Wh. Applying that 82% to 89% range to a 1,536 Wh label gives about 1,260 to 1,370 Wh at the outlet; that is my arithmetic, not a measurement of either 1,536 Wh unit.

findings.label: Measured efficiency
findings.source_title: Pecron E1500LFP portable power station review (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: The Solar Lab: 'achieved a 90% efficiency rating' in its testing, with an overheating warning during the test. The page does not define the method, name the reviewer or give a date. 0.90 × 1,536 Wh = about 1,382 Wh if this is discharge efficiency (my arithmetic).

findings.label: Measured AC charge time, empty to full
findings.source_title: Pecron E1500LFP portable power station review (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: The Solar Lab, wall outlet; it calls this 'slower than advertised'. Pecron's store page claims 1.8 hours (1 h 48 min).

findings.label: Output limit under test
findings.value: shut down when pushed past 2,200 W; the 4,400 W surge rating was not met
findings.source_title: Pecron E1500LFP portable power station review (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: The Solar Lab. It also reports the unit reached the full 800 W solar charge rate.

findings.label: Observed AC charge power
findings.value: about 1,300 W, full from empty in under 2 hours
findings.source_title: PECRON E1500LFP Expandable Power Station review (The Gadgeteer)
findings.note: Matt Gregersen, published 2024-01-23. A space heater spiked above 2,000 W and settled at about 1,500 W. No Wh-delivered or dB figure in the review.

findings.label: Observed loads
findings.value: kettle at almost 1,500 W took the battery from 84% to 78%; pressure washer at 1,000 to 1,450 W used roughly 30% in half an hour of on/off use
findings.source_title: Pecron E1500LFP Portable Power Station Hands-On Review: Lightning In A Box (The Drive)
findings.note: Michael Febbo, published 2024-08-08. Hands-on use, not a capacity test. He cites other reviews reporting 'over 1,400wh' output but did not measure it himself.

findings.label: Price at maker's US store
findings.source_title: PECRON E1500LFP Expandable Portable Power Station 2200W 1536Wh V3 Version
findings.note: Read with storecheck.py on 2026-11-11. $49 over the $500 cap. The page lists 1,536 Wh, 2,200 W, 3,500+ cycles to 80% and a warranty extended to 5 years with registration within 30 days.

findings.label: Measured capacity (OutdoorGearLab)
findings.note: Kenji Mowrey, published 2026-01-13. Light-bar test jig at 80% load until drained; '18% below its advertised 1,152 Wh'. Charge averaged 1.3 hours from 0% to full.

findings.label: Measured capacity (StorageReview)
findings.value: 1,030 Wh at a 350 W load; 1,360 Wh drawn from the wall for a 0 to 100% charge
findings.source_title: BLUETTI AC180 Portable Power Station Review (StorageReview)
findings.note: Kevin OBrien, published 2023-05-26. Inverter losses included. 1,030 ÷ 1,152 = 89% of rating; 1,030 ÷ 1,360 = 76% wall-to-outlet round trip (my arithmetic). Turbo charging drew 1,458 W.

findings.label: Measured capacity (Digital Trends)
findings.value: 976 Wh in a full discharge from 100%
findings.note: Simon Sage, published 2023-08-03. Measured with an Emporia smart plug. 976 ÷ 1,152 = 85% of rating (my arithmetic).

findings.label: Measured capacity and fan noise (Ken Rockwell)
findings.value: 943 Wh from the AC outlets; 1.37 kWh to recharge; 68.85% round trip; about 48 dBA at 1 m
findings.note: Ken Rockwell, page labelled October 2023, testing dated 24-29 August 2023. Discharge load not stated. The fan runs whenever AC output exceeds about 100 W. Standard charging at about 1,070 W took 1 h 21 min from 0 to 100%.

findings.label: Rival page check (willitrunpower.com)
findings.value: no measured figures; no ~1,500 Wh model
findings.source_title: Best power station under $500 (2026): picks by what you need to run | Willrun
findings.note: Runtimes are calculated as Wh × 0.85 ÷ (load + 15 W), an assumed factor. It lists the AC180 at $499 and out of stock at BLUETTI on Nov 8 (ships Dec 14).
